utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I remind you to tell it the truth as the affirmation still applies you made at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace unto this house with a wish that this trial and this day may end in keeping with God's will, not my will. I welcome the witness, and I wish her a pleasant day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My first question would be: Did you investigate that the BH Army corps had an analystical department dealing with intercepts, and if so, what is your knowledge and the knowledge of the teams of investigators about this analysis department? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you clarify what you mean by analystic department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the 2nd Corps of the BH Army in Tuzla have an analysis department analysing intercepts? Did they analyse intercepts, and do you know anything about it, because you waited almost three years to get those transcripts. Did you manage to find out if those transcripts had been analysed during the war and how?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the purpose of taking the intercepts was to send them to the 2 Corps for 2 Corps analysis by their intelligence unit. So, yes, they had -- my understanding is they had an analytical department that was responsible for analysing the intercepts as they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you as one of the investigators the Tribunal, because you were on the ground just after the events, had any contact with anyone from that analytical department, and did you ask them for access into those analyses, or did you perhaps seize the material that they had?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are a couple of different time periods that you mentioned in your question. One of them was immediately following the events. Immediately following the events, no one from the Office of the Prosecutor had contact, to my knowledge, with anybody in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to deal with the issue of reliability and authenticity of communications in light of the fact that this material was disclosed to you only in 1998, can you comment on this statement of the witness PW-32 from the transcript page 2176, lines 1 to 7. He said: "By the nature of things, each operator had to have insight into what was going on the ground. They knew these things by heart. Reports were analysed in detail by the analytical department, and based on those analyses instructions for further work were given." That's the end of the quotation. If there was any delay in the processing of the material, would this information given by the witness mean that there was actually no analysis of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the internal analysis that the army did of the intercepts, the Office of the Prosecutor was interested in the raw material so that we could look at the raw material. We, to my memory, received few analytical reports from the 2 Corps that for our purposes were not useful, relevant, or helpful, because we were interested in the raw material that was being collected at the time by the operators so that we could look at it on our own and make our own determination about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain what kind of analytical reports were available to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really basing this purely on memory. They would have been something like a synopsis that might have gone into a larger report. Some of the analytical information, also from memory, was of a tactical nature, very low-level, sort of Motorola snippets of conversations, and again nothing that was of significance or of relevance to our investigation because we were interested in looking at the raw material, not somebody else's version of what the raw material meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber when was the first time when you gained access to what you call raw material as far as intercepts are concerned.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On March 3rd, 1998, Jean-Rene Ruez took possession of a binder of approximately 550 intercepted conversations. Following that, in April of 1998, the Office of the Prosecutor took possession of 134 notebooks plus one additional notebook from 2 Corps. Also in April of 1998, the Office of the Prosecutor took possession of 19 audio reel-to-reel tapes from 2 Corps and also took possession of 13 reel-to-reel tapes from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did all this material relate to the events in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material in the binder that we received on the 3rd of March, 1998, did relate to the events of Srebrenica and Zepa. The time period of the material contained in that binder was from the 9th of July to the 31st of July, 1995. The material that we took possession of in the way of notebooks in April of 1998, I believe contained a broader range of dates and therefore would have contained information about events outside of those two events, namely Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, because you said you received binders, were those binders organised as these binders we handle here? Was this prepared for your use or was it unsorted material relating to certain events or perhaps sorted according to a certain chronology?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a single binder that we received that was sorted chronologically by date and time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. After taking possession of all this material that you mentioned in your previous answers starting from 3rd March 1998 onwards, did you or anyone from your team look into the possibilities, into the capacity of the BH Army and the 2nd Corps to intercept conversations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As has been stated, an expert from the US organisation called ATF, standing for Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, visited the two sites, examined the equipment, examined the antennas, and reported on the capability of units at those sites to intercept communication, and to intercept communication from the directions that they had indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, since you said that these were experts who analysed these capabilities, did they submit your report to you, the people in the Tribunal who engaged them to do this work?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this report contain any indicator of the capabilities of the BH Army on the southern and northern sites to select the information that was made available to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This expert, did he or she analyse the capability of the BH Army and the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina to intercept the communications on the air in the scope that is covered by the material made available to you? Were they capable of intercepting that amount of communications?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that you refer to the expert's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's no problem to refer to the report, but you as an investigator who looked into all of this, do you know if any expert report has been made about the capability of these particular teams at the southern and northern location with the number of personnel they had to intercept that amount of communications? Did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My memory also is that one of the intercept operators noted that he thought that there would have been even more communication than what there was given the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The record doesn't show that my question included also this: Was the number of personnel at southern and northern locations realistically sufficient to collect all this information in that period of time? I would like the number of personnel to be recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the number of personnel and I believe there have been a number of radio intercept operators including squad leaders and commanders who have been here to testify who could give you a much more accurate number; but my recollection is that each of the operators was responsible for working on at least a couple of the reel-to-reel machines at a time and therefore could record at least a couple of conversations at a time and had the ability while recording to also continue to listen to further conversations. In this way, they were able to monitor several channels and several frequencies at any one time. On top of that, if you consider that there were two sites and at one site that there were three units working, I believe there were sufficient personnel and equipment to record the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. From your discussions with operators, are you aware that they had at most three recorders at one facility and only one at the other facility? Do you know that from taking interviews from the operators, from doing interviews?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my memory of what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of direct examination, you made the assertion that intercepts were used in realtime. On page 5000 in this case, lines 1 to 13 of 7 September this year, you said: "They used the material in realtime to forward it to their command posts or to protect their personnel, or they conveyed the information they considered relevant." If you look at that page of the transcript, do you think I quoted you correctly? Can you remember what you said?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any evidence or any indicators showing that the intercepted communications were used by the BH Army in realtime and that the army indeed acted to protect its personnel by passing on the information contained in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One example comes to mind, and I'm referring to a summary of an Excel table of intercepted communication relating to this case. The one conversation that comes to mind is one that I believe took place on the 15th of July in which Semso Muminovic, one of the Bosnian military commanders, and Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, were in touch with each other, Muminovic trying to get in touch with Pandurevic in order to create a corridor so that the column could get through. I believe that the contact began on the 15th of July, and I believe that the -- that a corridor was opened on the 16th of July. I could confirm this by going through these documents. And then I believe this is further verified by a written report that Vinko Pandurevic wrote on the 17th of July. This information came through not only in one conversation here, but it came through also from, I believe, the president's office through to the Main Staff who was then informed of Pandurevic's actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this information gained by virtue of the fact that Semso Muminovic and Vinko Pandurevic informed their superiors about their conversation or because intercepts were recorded by operators as taking place at a certain time, on a certain date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am asking you, in fact, about the speed of conveyance of this information passed by operators to the users in the BH Army, Alija Izetbegovic, Rasim Delic, and other decision-makers. Do you have any evidence that these decision-makers in the BH Army actually ever received any of this information contained in intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's a question that would be more appropriately put to a different witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because in your evidence here, like all the operators, focus on the noting of information into a notebook or a transcript, but nobody mentions the fact that this information was supposed to be passed on for operative use to those who made decisions. Did you investigate whether this information ever came into the hands of users at a higher level, people who made decisions, at any level?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were told in the course of the interviews and investigation was that once the material was written down in the notebook, it was typed up and it was sent to their headquarters for further action. From our standpoint as a member of the Office of the Prosecutor investigating the events of Srebrenica and Zepa, what was important, again, was the raw information so that we could work with it and develop it independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know if the end users ever saw that information, or did they see it only here after this trial, after your presentation and the presentations of the Defence teams at trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I wasn't an end user.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you answer this: In the binders that you have before you during your testimony as well as all the other operators who testify here, they also have similar binders. Do they contain a written proof that the information was used by the end user such as the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Izetbegovic, or Rasim Delic and his associates or end users of that kind and at that level? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a single intercepted conversation which was obtained from the level of the army, the Presidency after their processing and the order as to what to do in view of the fact that they were privy to such information? Do you have any such thing in the files of the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember an intercept on the 12th of July in which the military, VRS military, was asking for buses and trucks from specific municipalities. The Office of the Prosecutor then obtained orders from the Ministry of Defence from Republika Srpska. I believe they were two different orders that detailed the need for buses and trucks from precisely the same municipalities as specified in the radio communication that came through on the 12th of July, captured by the Bosnian military from VRS personnel on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to the intercepts of the BiH Army, were they intended for use by users in Republika Srpska or, rather, by users in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically by users of -- by users in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, could you say whether during the investigation of those documents and during reading, diligently reading those documents, could you notice that any of the documents had been studied by any of the officers from the General Staff of the BH Army or the presidency of BiH, did they make a note on any of them? Did they append an order or an instruction on -- of any kind on the margin of such a document if there was indeed such a document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who made notations, but I believe that on some of the printouts that we initially received there were some handwritten notations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The printed examples that you're mentioning, have they been included in the binders and shown to the Trial Chamber, and also, has the Office of the Prosecutor disclosed such documents to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, but the witness has already started answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in terms of the disclosure obligations of the Prosecution, I don't know that that's an appropriate question to put to the witness since the witness was not part of the pre-trial proceedings with respect to this case. So I think that's a completely inappropriate question to put to this witness. In terms of whether they exist or not, that's a completely separate issue, but in terms of whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor disclosed that to the Defence in this case, it's not something that this witness is privy to, and I think the accused is well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are in the best position to answer this question: What was disclosed to you and your Defence team? And if that material was complete or not, you should discuss with the Prosecution. They have the obligation to disclose the material and what they have, and that should be discussed among the parties. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. I no longer need an answer to my question. Could the court please produce P787 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the document in the Serbian language, and since you speak Serbian, while we're waiting for the English version I can still ask. In the Serbian version you can see that it says -- there's a remark by the chief who requested the information and the name of the person that he sent the letter to, and that person's name is Eso. This document was disclosed by the Defence, and that's why I asked whether you've seen a transcript of an intercepted conversation with similar annotations on the margins appended by a superior officer or an officer from a superior command. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the right-hand side corner it says "A/A." That's ad acta, something used by people speaking the language that both you and I speak, A/A standing for ad acta. Every document has to show that it has been filed, and a superior officer has to include an instruction to the archives as to how the document would be kept.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we have a look at another document, which is P788. Thank you. We see it on the screen now. The title is "OA." This is the abbreviation in the Serbian language. OA stands for an operative operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Did you ever see a document pertaining to this operative operation conducted by the intelligence department under the code-name The Truth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember seeing any such document or reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You see Chief Brigadier General Jusuf Jasarevic says whatever he said, and he sent this document to the command of 2 Corps, and the officer in the 2 Corps command wrote: "Check where the -- who's got these audio recordings." Hajro wrote that and that was also translated into English. I'm sure you can see it and you can see the signature of the superior officer who instructs his subordinate as to what to do with the document. This document was used by the Defence during your examination and tendered it into evidence in its present form, and this also confirms that there indeed was an operative action under the name Truth. Did you notice this during your analysis of the documents that were made available to you on the 18th of August? Did the Prosecutor ever investigate the operative action Truth conducted by the 2 Corps -- or, rather, its intelligence and security department? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and the 18th of August of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: 1995. We analysed this document last week. I don't want to go into its content. My intention was to show you that the superior officer always put something on the margin in order to instruct his -- his subordinates about the documents. Since you've seen the documents with annotations on the margins, did you see any of the intercepts that you are testifying about here as a witness with such handwritten added annotations on the margins? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there were handwritten annotations on the margins, the ones that I was referring to a few minutes back would have been on the margins of that original binder of 550 pages. My memory is that there were some handwritten notes on those pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, on page 13, line 8, your words were recorded by: "This document was used by the Defence during your examination and tendered into evidence ..." I don't think that -- because it's a P document that the Defence used it and tendered it. It was the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I said that the Defence used this exhibit in the examination of the witness last week, and this document can be found in the Prosecutor's file, and it bears an ERN number, 0261655. I just wanted to demonstrate an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But it was not tendered by the Defence but by the Prosecution. I just wanted to clarify this. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did not want to discuss this. I just wanted to show some examples for the witness's benefit, to show her what margins are and what annotations on the margins are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber whether you as an investigator of this Tribunal investigated why all the documents that are presented here in trials against different accused originate from the company for interception, and there's no single document that would originate from other command levels within the BiH Army, including the documents that have been presented to you during your trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that that statement fundamentally misstates the record of these proceedings. The accused is well aware that the intercept information came from a number of sources. He's cross-examined witnesses from the 2nd Corps. He's cross-examined witnesses -- or at least a witness from the 21st Division. He's cross-examined witnesses from the State Security Services, and I think that to -- to represent to this witness in any shape or form that all of the documents came from the 2nd Corps fundamentally is incorrect, and I think it places the witness at an unfair advantage. And if he has a precise question, I'd ask that he frame it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tolimir, what do you mean by "that have been presented to you during your trial"? What do you mean by that? It was recorded that way. Perhaps you rephrase your question and put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll rephrase indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is there a single intercepted conversation that has been presented to you during your testimony and the testimonies you provided during the Popovic and Krstic trials that originates from a different level and excludes those at north and south site and the companies at those sites? And there's no other level in -- in the BiH Army or the state security of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As an investigator, does this mean to you that the analysis has not been done thoroughly, that it hasn't been complete since it has taken into account only the lowest level, the first level of interception, the intercept operator, that is, and nobody else?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the contrary. I think starting at that level is the most authentic level to begin at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you all this because you yourself have claimed that intercepts were analysed in realtime. Could you please focus on my next question. Could an end user at the level of the BiH Army and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina be provided with information in realtime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we define realtime in a matter of minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the Prosecutor have and did you as an investigator see a single piece of evidence that demonstrates that Alija Izetbegovic or Rasim Delic indeed used those intercepts in realtime, or any other members of the command of the Main Staff of the BiH Army or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the focus of my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How can you claim, then, that they were able to deal with those documents in realtime in view of the fact that you did not investigate that, that you did not see a single piece of evidence that would prove that? What is your basis for claiming that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you refer to the packet of information that we've been discussing, tabs 1 through 12, it contains information intercepted by the SDB and corroborated by other services. That information, some of the information contained in there, had to do with, for example, the spelling of the deceased Dutch UNPROFOR soldier's name and his tag number in order to allow his body to be transported from Bratunac to Zvornik to Tuzla to Split. That information was conveyed in realtime, and the body, in fact, was transported. There are many other examples like that that we could go through in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether that information you -- that the intercept operator at south or north front was conveyed to either me or General Nicolai who were involved in the arrangements to transport the body from Bratunac to Zagreb and further on, and what has that got to do with the end users in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that we were talking about the ability to convey information in realtime, and that was my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you as an investigator know that intelligence services must convey information in zero time to any end user at the highest level? Yes or no? I hope that you are aware of that. I'm sure that you are.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what zero time is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Zero time is the time that does not suffer a difference from information received to information conveyed to the end user. That means that information has to be available in zero time to the end user who commissioned the collection of data by means of intercepted conversations. That's zero time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I would like to hear the answer first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It seems to me from the way this is going that the witness is talking at cross-purposes with respect to the questions that are put by the accused in this case, and that stems from, I think, properly defining or properly circumscribing what is meant by the term "realtime" analysis. Whether that is just processing, whether that is conveying information or whether or not that is recording information that is being conveyed, and I think because of that we're having answers that don't necessarily correspond to the questions and questions that don't necessarily correspond to the answers. I would ask if Mr. Tolimir could be more precise in terms of framing his questions so that we can avoid this kind of misunderstanding. The witness has answered the accused on a number of occasions citing examples where intercepts have recorded information that has been conveyed in relatively short order from -- concerning the subject matter of which the intercept is speaking about, but that responds to a different question than what Mr. Tolimir is putting, which is whether or not the information that is being recorded is being conveyed within the security chain or within whatever chain it's being analysed to the authorities upon which to act. So I think if -- if we can frame the question more precisely, we probably will get clearer answers and we'll also get, I think we'll -- we'll go forward in a more efficient way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this recommendation, but I think it's up to the accused to phrase his question in that way or in another way. He might have something in mind which leads him to phrase a question in that way he did it, and I think this witness is capable to answer in an appropriate way. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here's an example for the witness that she will understand and she will know what zero time is. For example, a broker buying shares in a stock market and a company goes bust and he buys its shares after he has learned that the company has gone bust. Is he going to be rewarded or punished by his employer? The situation is very similar in the intelligence service. For example, if I or the 2 Corps of the BiH Army collects information, will we be rewarded if we submit information that we gathered after the activity that we surveil is over? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is -- in fact, I was trying to explain to the witness what zero time means. If a broker at a stock market finds out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's not necessary to repeat that. I understood your explanation. My question is what was your question to this witness related to her experience during her time in the OTP? What is your question to this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. She said she did not understand what zero time means. I can give her another example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Would information collected by interceptors -- I am asking the question. Would information collected by interceptors at the northern and southern site be passed on to Rasim Delic or Alija Izetbegovic within five to ten minutes so that they could react to it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want a clarification from General Tolimir. At page 19 of today's transcript, lines 8 to 10, you give an example and you say: "For example, if I or the 2 Corps of the BiH Army collects information, will we be rewarded if we submit information after the activity that we surveil is over?" Is that a question or a statement? I know there is question mark at the end, but is that what happens, or you're asking a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking a question. For instance, if somebody collects information about the events in Srebrenica, would that person be rewarded for getting that information in the event that his superior had not received it until after the events were over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's leave this framework of the specific work you did. D48, page 9 of the book, paragraph 2. Let's see what other people say about this. When we get the document, I'll read the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still don't have it. D48, page 46 in e-court. Page 299 of the book, paragraph 2. I will read the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the right page in e-court. The text highlighted in red. "The question that now needs to be answered is what was possible regarding the processing of the intercepts in realtime? Simple arithmetic shows that if the number of channels multiplied by the number of required personnel is greater than the number of available personnel, then near realtime processing and reporting is impossible." And five lines below it reads: "If we assume on the basis of this estimate that an absolute minimum of ten channels had to be monitored continuously, that three persons were needed per channel for interception, transcription and reporting, and that there was a rotation of three shifts a day and seven-day working week, then at least 90 Signit operators would have had to be active at the site, not to mention 15 or 20 staff for support, technology, security, catering, and so on. Hence, if there were 20 channels, probably a more realistic estimate, then at least 180 people would be needed. In reality a maximum of ten people worked in the northern location. Most of the communication was recorded on tape. It seems, therefore, that near realtime analysis and processing was unattainable." My question is: Could you give us your comment as an investigator on this analysis of the realistic state of affairs at this site presented by the author of this book?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time that I saw this was on Friday when it was presented. I have not read it, and so what I know of it is what has been put here on the screen. Just as a cursory sort of reaction to it, I would say that there are many assumptions that are made here that in fact are not truly based on the reality of the situation at the time. Furthermore, not all conversations were considered to be very urgent. Some of them were, and those conversations were marked as such on the conversations themselves, and they were typed up immediately, and they were forwarded to the command posts. There were certainly many conversations that were also missed, and this is evidence in a few conversations that we see in the tabs in the 12 conversations presented in this pamphlet of information that we've been looking at where sometimes the Croatians picked up a conversation that the Bosnian authorities missed. The Croatians picked it up, and this other source that the Tribunal now has also picked it up, but the ABiH did not pick it up. So certainly there were also conversations that they did not pick up. This is not -- what we have is not an absolutely complete, 24-hour, seven-day-a-week set of conversations. It's as many conversations as they could pick up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking you is this: We have seen quotes from the report on Srebrenica of the Dutch Institute for War Documentation. It's a very serious and voluminous analysis which you can read and then make the conclusion that you just made, but my question is: Did the OTP analyse at all how many people were needed on the southern and northern location to be able to monitor the radio network of the Army of Republika Srpska at the time of the events in Srebrenica and Zepa, to intercept them and transcribe them in realtime, to put them into notebooks and on paper and pass this on to their immediate superiors and up to the highest level of command?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the OTP investigate, since you had to wait a long time for these transcripts from 1995 until you finally got them in 2005, did you investigate whether reports were made of this capability based on Croatian or American sources who were monitoring the air at the time with their drones and satellites?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we discussed this on Friday, and I mentioned that we had tried to approach other governments and that we received very little. We received enough to know that they had information but not enough to be able to compare it against the information that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In any case, the OTP didn't get them, as you claim, but is it possible that the BH Army got information from others who had such information, and were they able to analyse it over the course of the four years that you've been working for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that's a question that's more suited to a different witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then tell us whether the Office of the Prosecutor has in its possession information on the total number of intercepts in Srebrenica and Zepa at the critical time, the time covered by this indictment?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a precise number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you knew that because you were an investigator dealing exclusively with that material. But here is another question: Did you as OTP investigators review notebooks on intercepts and note that there were interruptions, blank spaces in communications for certain days?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll try, if I can remember what I asked, but it would be easier for you to read the transcript. The question was: When you investigators of this Tribunal reviewed the transcripts, did you find any gaps? Did you establish how many days there were when no intercepts were recorded?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the period between the events -- well, let's just say July of 1995, I do not believe there are any gaps. And with respect to the notebooks, if there were gaps, as you call them, in the notebooks between one day and another, that is explained by the fact that there were several notebooks at any one location at any one time that were being used. So a notebook may just simply be set aside for a day and maybe nobody wrote in that notebook, but they did write in other notebooks, and therefore there were conversations that were intercepted and transmitted to their headquarters on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You just mentioned notebooks, and that's the material you studied. You said yourself that some days are blank. However, it is claimed here in court that the transcripts are authentic because they were written in longhand in notebooks. Now, I'm asking you, is it possible that for these days there are gaps, you just didn't receive information, or there was no interception in those days?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was interception in those days. It's just that the conversations were recorded in other notebooks also located at that site. As I mentioned, there were several notebooks that the operators would work with. It was possible that one notebook would be set aside for a day or two days but that those conversations were still being recorded and transcribed in other notebooks at that same site and then transmitted electronically to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You already answered my question. Was it possible for two or three operators to intercept within one day such a number of conversations, transcribe them and send them to their commands, all this amount of information contained in several notebooks? Could all this have been done with just two or three operators at any one site?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would need to go through the duty log-book to see who was working on which days, but I think it's a misrepresentation to say that there were only two or three operators that were working at any one site during those days. I have no reason to doubt that those operators were able to intercept, transcribe, and send the conversations as they were recorded in the notebooks and forwarded to their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I put to you what has been heard here by the OTP and the Trial Chamber from the operators themselves. They said they worked in shifts of two. Now, the OTP received a great number of these notebooks you just mentioned where these intercepts are recorded. In addition, Witness PW-32 said on page 2184, lines 19 through 25: "When I arrived at the unit, my job was, first of all, to put some order into work. This notebook is the result of that effort. I'm certain that a whole truckload of such notebooks was burned because we had no firewood." My question is: Did the BH at the northern and southern sites, with such a small number of operators, have the possibility to fill a truck with notebooks that were burnt eventually? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on another witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But it's a fact relating to the actual state of affairs at the site where this witness worked. He said a full truckload of such notebooks had been burned. Anyway, I appreciate your answer. I will quote to you further what this witness, PW-32, said at page 2182, lines 21 through 25: "All these notebooks before we started to use them were registered. They would get a number and a date, and they were marked 'strictly confidential,' and they would be sent to the northern or southern site." My question to you is: Did you check these registration numbers on the notebooks, because I've seen here that some of them do not have numbers? And can you tell us what could be the reason why they would be marked and treated as official documentation and then later burned?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I remember is that when the members of the Office of the Prosecutor first found the notebooks at the northern site that the ABiH person with them was embarrassed that they were not kept in an orderly manner, and then that he also said, "Actually, we shouldn't even have these anymore."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that they were destroyed, thrown away, burned?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone from the OTP saw these notebooks at the northern location, did they not want to take them, seize them, use them in the trials conducted here?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the notebooks that we've been using.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These notebooks that we've been using in my trial, I looked at them and they are very neatly written. There is nothing crossed out, or almost nothing, in just one or two intercepts. How can you explain that with such speed that their work required they were able to write so neatly? Did you investigate the notebooks from that point of view?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see in the notebooks that there are passages crossed out or where intercept operators started to transcribe something and then just crossed out the whole thing and started again. They listened to the tapes bit by bit, and given their experience in listening, they were able to transcribe them bit by bit by rewinding the reel-to-reel, playing it, rewinding it, playing it, rewinding it, playing it, and then -- and transcribing the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you answer this question: Since all the operators that we've heard in this trial stated that they wrote in those notebooks exclusively for their own use to record the conversations from the tape and they did not send these notebooks to end users, could you tell us whether they would be so careful to write neatly and avoid crossing things out, considering that these notebooks were not going to be sent anywhere, nor marked for good work?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them had better handwriting than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you look into the possibility that the writing in this -- these notebooks was actually copied from pieces of paper or something like that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that before this system of employing the notebooks was put into place, they, in fact, did write on pieces of paper and that from December of 1994, they started to use the notebooks. Whether or not they sometimes used pieces of paper, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know that they started using notebooks beginning with December 1994?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my memory from speaking with the person who instituted that change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any notebooks from that period so that we could look at them and check the veracity of that statement? Did the Office of the Prosecutor receive material from before that time and after that time so we can compare?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any notebooks with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the time when there were certain gaps in the notebooks. In fact, you said there were no gaps, and I claim there are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at P40, which is a report from the southern location referring to jamming of certain frequencies. In fact, it's P540, and it should not be broadcast because of the heading which refers to the name of the two locations. Let us just redact or not show the -- the title of the document and show the rest. Thank you. We have it in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a report precisely from an intercepting facility. It says: "On the order to jam the following frequencies: 261.350, 266.925, 246.725, 266.550 and others located in the assigned direction. "We are faced with several problems. The batteries to which we attach the Mini kobac radio equipment set are made of steel, a leftover of the UN. Everyone knows that they are of lower voltage than lead batteries, which means that with them we cannot obtain the voltage necessary to activate the transmitter. Sometimes we manage, but sometimes we don't. "At any rate, the batteries are dilapidated. "The rectifier, which we are supposed to use to charge them, emits a maximum of 15.5 volts, which is insufficient to power the Mini kobac transmitter, which has a built-in automatic switch which blocks it if the voltage is too low. By the way, the transformer on the rectifier, which we borrowed from signals operators for our purposes, shorted today. Another problem is the shortage of operators which could be resolved somehow on a short-term basis, but it is in our nature to ask for work when there isn't anything and no one to do it with." This is a report from the 27th May 1995, and my question is: When a certain frequency's jammed, do you also monitor communications on that frequency concerning -- in view of the fact that the signal of the jamming device is stronger than the signal of the frequency being monitored and you cannot hear anything on the air because the jamming interferes with all the communications. Would that perhaps explain the gaps in intercepts? Did you see any evidence of that in the material you looked at?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you started your question, you said that I said that there were no gaps. In fact, I said it's possible, and, in fact, my memory is that there were gaps in some of the notebooks. Your link between those gaps in a few notebooks I have explained in a different way, that the operators put the notebooks aside. They had several notebooks that they were working with, and that there in fact by date were no gaps, so to speak. With respect to this report, I cannot comment. I do not have the technical capacity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's over time now. We need the first break. We are in the same position as the intercept operators. The tapes have to be rewound in this courtroom as well, and therefore we need the technical break, and we will resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we are back to the process of scrambling. That was described in the document dated 27 -- 25th of July [as interpreted], 1995, and this document says that the operators did not have adequate equipment that would enable them to work 24/7. Please, did you in the Office of the Prosecutor investigate -- investigate the consequences of jamming the signal on tapping in communications, and did it have any impact on the way conversations were intercepted during the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such technical knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it necessary for the Tribunal to investigate the lack of information during the period when the signals were jammed, and how did that reflect at looking at the real situation only from the point of view of the communications segment?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the last sentence you saw, and I'll quote again, it says: "The custom is to look for work when there is no work to be had." And the last sentence that I just read out to you, does it say that in the site there were very low possibilities, the capabilities were almost nonexistent for work, because in this sentence he also says, "We have nobody to work with nor anything to work on." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I am lost at the moment. Could you help me and indicate from which document you were quoting. Was it the last document, P540, or what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document is indeed P540, and it is still on the screen -- or, rather, it is not on the screen. I actually can see it, it's on the left-hand side of the screen. It's in the Serbian language and the English translation is missing. I quoted from the last sentence of that document, and I will repeat: "... but it is in our nature to ask for work when there isn't anything and no one to do it with." And then I asked the witness whether such situation in the facility, which was the lack of equipment and personnel, did it have any impact on the quality of tapping into the phone conversations and the volume of the recorded and transcribed materials. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there was a typo in line 30 -- line 25 in respect to the date of this document. It was recorded, I think, above as the 27th of July, 1995, or the 25th of July, 1995, where it should say the 27th of May, 1995. This is the first time that I've seen this document, and I don't have any technical capacity to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for having corrected the date for the record. I don't want to go back to the date because the document contains the name of the facility, and I will no longer need this document on the screen since you say that you've not seen it before. I'm just saying that this is a means of proof that there -- that radio conversations were jammed, and I wanted to demonstrate what the reactions were to such things at the facility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court now please produce P289 in e-court. This is a record on the hand-over of the archive materials concerning the events in Srebrenica in 1995, more specifically the hand-over of audiotape to Mr. Jack Hunter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I was just told the last document we have just had on the screen, P540, is not in evidence yet. It was marked for identification when it was used by the Prosecution with Witness PW-030. Are you tendering this document now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We thought that it was already in evidence. If not, I would like to tender it because it's a document unto itself, and it's self-explanatory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received. And I think with the P number, P540. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Serbian document be moved to the right to allow me to read from it, because I don't see the beginnings of the lines in document. Thank you. It's enough now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, based on the document that you are most probably familiar with because you did speak about Mr. Jack Hunter who took the tapes to the US Army, could you please explain for the Trial Chamber who Jack Hunter is and why in the fourth paragraph in this document it says "Jack Hunter" and then initials "LR-US Army," and below his signature we are can see "ATT." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a typographical error in the document that Jack Hunter was a member of the US Army. As you pointed out, underneath his signature he specifies ATF, which is miswritten in the translation. In the translation is says "ATAF." ATF stands for the Agency for Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms in the United States. That's the agency that Jack Hunter worked for as an expert in electronic recognizance processing of these tapes, and his -- he also had expertise in antennas and being able to pick up radio signals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a question. Is this organisation a state institution or is it a private company, or is it an NGO? Can you explain a little bit further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a US agency, US government agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for her answer and corrections made to the document. Now, could you kindly tell us whether this organisation, ATS [as interpreted], as you called it, an organisation that Jack Hunter worked for, is it a part of the armed forces of the US or of another big organisation? Could you briefly describe the status of that organisation for us?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a part of the US military, and I do not know which -- whether it falls under its own department or whether it falls under a different department within the US government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And before 2003, was that organisation part of the Ministry of Justice of the United States of America or the Treasury? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if Mr. Hunter worked also for the armed forces of the USA, and during his contacts with army representatives, did he introduce himself as a member of the US Army? And I'm asking you this because of the fourth paragraph where there are initials coupled with the US Army, and there is also W-ABH. What does that stand for? Before you answer, could you please bear in mind that it is impossible that there are two typos or three typos in the same document, in the first paragraph, in the third paragraph, and -- so my question, to cut a long story short, is whether he was a member of the US Armed Forces, and did he introduce himself as such?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, he wasn't a member of the armed forces, and I don't know whether he would have introduced himself as such. I don't remember him introducing himself as such, but I don't have any knowledge of him being a member of the US Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I respect it when you say that there are things you don't remember and when you're honest about it. Could you please tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the -- on the -- on the left-hand side I can only read the names. The signatures on both lines look the same to me. I don't know whose signature that is, but on the left-hand side it says "Handed over by Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic, signed," and then it says underneath that, "Major Sevko Tihic, signed." On the right-hand side it is signed by Jack Hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that the signatories signed something that was never said to them and then it was erroneously translated into passages that he was an army member, or perhaps he was an army member and that he introduced himself as such?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he signed something erroneously, because underneath his name he indicates "ATF," which stands for Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms. He did not speak the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there interpreters there? Were you there when he signed this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether there were interpreters there, whether I was there. It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now move on to the following question. Look at the fourth paragraph where it says: "The administration for intelligence and security during the hand-over of other tapes should listen to select and approve the other tapes for use." Were you able to follow that in -- in English?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You did not read it in English, or you did read it in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you have read this, could you please tell us whether the tapes were listened to by either yourself or the signatories in the intelligence and security administration, and did you attend the exercise of listening to those tapes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the tapes were taken immediately by Jack Hunter to the United States for analysis so that he could make copies of them and return them to me -- or to the Office of the Prosecutor. I listened to some of the tapes, but I did not listen to all of the tapes and all of the conversations in the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the passage carefully, especially the words in brackets where it says, "The intelligence and security administration, the tapes should be listened to and selected, and the matter of the further use of these tapes should be resolved, the emphasis being on the remainder of the tapes," this remark in brackets refers to the remainder of tapes and their use. What is the selection referred to in here, and what is the matter of the further use of the remainder of the tapes that is referred to in here, and all that was to be resolved at the moment when the tapes were handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. I think that the section that says "and the matter of the further use of the tapes should be resolved" refers to whether or not the Office of the Prosecutor would be given permission to use them in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The selection here, does it apply to you as end users, or those who provided the tapes to you, were they the ones who made the original selection as to what tapes to give you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had identified 19 tapes, and we asked for all of them, and there were an additional 13 tapes that had been identified in Sarajevo that we also asked for and received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this: Do you perhaps remember whether at the administration, because it says here "the intelligence and security administration, the tapes should be listened to and selected and the matter of the remainder of the tapes should be resolved," and I emphasise the word "remainder," the rest of the tapes. Does this mean that the signatures -- all the signatures were involved in the selection process and making the decision on the further use of those tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we received the interpretation "the remainder." In the English translation we see on the screen there is not the -- I don't see the word "remainder," but, "the matter of the further use of the tapes should be resolved." Perhaps we have here a problem of interpretation or content, I don't know, but I don't see the word "remainder." That indicates slightly different content than the further use of something. Perhaps you can elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm reading the original document which was signed by the representatives of the BiH Army and Mr. Hunter, and I'm reading the text that they signed, and in it it says "the remainder of the tapes." And the witness confirmed that there were other tapes save for the 19 which are indicated here. The witness speaks Serbian. Maybe she should read what it says in the original because I believe that the translation is wrong. The prevalent copy is the one that has been signed in the original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, do you have any explanation for the problem which has occurred related to the interpretation? Can you read this part of the original document in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that Mr. Tolimir is referring to the line in the middle of paragraph 4 where it says: "When taking possession of the other tapes ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hmm. So maybe that's the confusion that Mr. Tolimir is referring to, the first sentence of the fourth paragraph where -- I also thought that he was referring to the second-to-the-last paragraph where it says: "The matter of the further use of the tapes should be resolved." He's referring to the first paragraph which says: "With the obligation that when taking possession of the other tapes," I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look carefully, it says: "The intelligence and security administration, when taking possession of the other tapes, shall listen to the tapes and select them and decide," et cetera, et cetera. So the administration took it upon itself to select what other tapes they will let you have, to listen to them and to decide on the further use of these tapes. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory is that, yes, they made a selection in order to ensure that the material we were going to be given related to the time period that we were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it possible that in the course of this selection they left out what they thought undesirable for you to have and that they left only what they wanted you to have?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a possibility. I would say that it's also important to keep in mind that the tapes were in short supply during the war, and therefore they were taped over many times. Therefore, we ended up with some conversations on tape that we could reference to the handwritten notebooks, but it wasn't by any means a complete collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Because you said yourself it is a possibility that they made a selection, is it also possible that they erased some of the conversations they thought to be unimportant, irrelevant, et cetera? Is it possible they gave you only those intercepts which they thought to be important and relevant?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part of your question is: "Is it also possible that they erased some of the conversations they thought to be unimportant, irrelevant, et cetera?" I would say, yes, certainly they did, because there was a shortage of tapes. So if they didn't consider something to be important or relevant, they would tape over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since this hand-over was done and this document was signed on the 29th April 1998, when the war was over and the Dayton Accords had been signed, was it still relevant that there was a short supply of tapes and that somebody was re-taping?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is relevant, because the tapes were made in 1995 when the war was still going on, and it was during that time that they had to re-tape conversations, tape over conversations because there was a shortage of tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This note that we just read, does it relate to 1995 or 1998 when you were signing this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jack Hunter signed it in 1998 for material that was recorded in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This selection, then, that was done in 1998, was it -- was it done after the war, after the signing of the Dayton Accords, or in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1998, after this agreement was signed, did this intelligence and security administration tamper or in any way manipulate these tapes that were handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would refer you to Jack Hunter's report. To my knowledge, there was no such evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This relates to tapes other than those taken by Jack Hunter, but if you mention Jack Hunter, we'll deal with that now. On transcript page 4982, lines 16 and 17, you said that Jack Hunter took those tapes to his laboratory in Washington, made copies and returned them together with the originals. Did he return both copies and originals, and why did he take them to his lab in Washington?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is going back -- back a long time for me and my memory is not crystal clear on it. I will -- I'm happy to tell you what I can remember. Mr. Hunter took those tapes to his -- to the ATF laboratory in Washington to be able to enhance some of the original recordings so that they could be heard better. He needed the originals in order to be able to do this. Eventually, he returned them to us along with copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind what you just said, that Jack Hunter took those tapes and took them to the lab of his agency, ATF, to enhance the audibility, can you tell me, if you know, did Jack Hunter, when he was making this analysis, write a report on it, and does that report exist somewhere in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether Jack Hunter had to make a request to his agency, which you call ATF, or to the Ministry of Justice or to the Treasury or the army, because we've seen he worked for all of them, a request to make these copies and to work on these tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know if any erasing was done in this laboratory? Can you be sure that none of the recordings were damaged or erased?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to your last question, I have to -- I'd like to say two things. One, I have to assume that his agency knew, because he was sent by ATF and he was a representative of ATF. So he would not have come simply on his own. His agency had to have known that he came, that he was asked to come, and that he was doing this work. Again, I think it's -- the fact -- you mentioned that he's in the army. I think that this is a typo in the document, and I would just like to respect that. At least to my knowledge. As to whether or not the tapes were erased in his laboratory, I don't believe that we received back any blank tapes. It's hard for me to imagine that such a thing would have happened in the ATF lab, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this honest answer, but now -- because you've just said that Hunter came down there on behalf of his organisation ATF; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the Tribunal requested an expert to come and assist us with material, because we had no internal expertise. Therefore, a request was made to the US government to provide an expert that could help us out with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's the US government who decided who this expert would be.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in identifying him or recruiting him or contacting ATF, so I don't know what the process was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said more than once during your evidence that you were not able to decipher certain tapes and that all this equipment was European made, the recorders, the UHERs, and everything else. Why wasn't this expertise provided by European institutions and laboratories that are closer to The Hague such as German, Swiss, and others which provided the equipment in the first place? Germany, for instance, has very good technology for analysing tapes and disks containing recordings made also on machines that they produce.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your statement says that I said more than once during my evidence that -- that I or we were unable to decipher certain tapes. I don't believe that I said that. I may have said that there were certain parts of tapes that were inaudible. As for why the Tribunal decided not to ask an expert from a European institution or laboratory, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke, but I heard when we discussed the diskettes given to you by the State Security Service that you were not able to decipher some of them. Perhaps it was misinterpreted, or perhaps I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two different mediums. The diskettes had to do with electronic versions of the transcripts that we were unable to open. The audiotapes are a second medium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question to the question of Tolimir. You said on page 43, line 2, 1 and 2: "I believe the Tribunal requested an expert to come and assist us with material, because we had no internal expertise." What are you referring to when you are saying, "We had no internal expertise"? In which field? Could you explain that a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had no one in house who could visit the two radio intercept sites, look at antennae, look at transmitters, look at receivers, look at the tape-recording equipment and analyse it and discuss whether it had the capacity to pick up the radio communication from the locations as had been described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there in Europe any experts that could have done what was done eventually in Washington, and was it necessary to take the tapes to Washington?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly there are experts in Europe in this field. I think it was a simple matter of members of the Office of the Prosecutor having contacts with ATF and reaching out because it was the easiest and quickest way to find an expert. I would just correct on the transcript page 45, line 2. It says in this "feel." It should say in this "field." Thank you. I would also delete "had." In the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us, this work done by Mr. Hunter for the Tribunal, does it fall under Rule 70 on access to material, or in other words, banning access to evidence to all persons save for those authorised by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. Maybe the Prosecutor can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to Mr. Hunter's reports, we don't consider that Rule 70 material, and indeed it has been disclosed to the accused. It was disclosed on 7 March 2008. That was a report dated 23 March 1998. There was another one that was dated 24th April 1998, and a third dated 24th April 1998. Those are some photographs actually, the last reference refers to photographs that were attached to the second report that I indicated. So all of those materials were disclosed to the accused in 2008 and they're not Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies the situation. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank the witness and the Prosecutor for the -- the answer, but I didn't want an answer about these tapes. I want an answer about the communication between the Tribunal and Mr. Hunter. I was asking if that was the reason why he was chosen over an expert in Europe, for instance, but we'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
