utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the process of examining these tapes on the premises of Mr. Hunter and his agency, was an expert report made to explain how these tapes were obtained, what results were obtained by reviewing them and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, as an investigator, is it customary for material handed over for expertise, like in this case, because Mr. Hunter was an expert, in the framework of a trial, is it customary for an expert report to be made and later submitted to the Trial Chamber and the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe the Prosecutor can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, because our time is running out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up P838. It's marked for identification because there is no Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the first page in the English original, and now we can seat same page in the Serbian language. The document is dated 17 October 2000. Let's look at the part before the signatures, the last paragraph. "This is to certify that I received a copy of the attached inventory consisting of four pages listing 20 items and that it is a true and accurate record of the items obtained pursuant to the consensual search conducted by the above named persons of the ICTY between 1830 and 0400 hours on the 16th and 17th October 2000 at Ramiz Salcin Barracks, Otoka, Sarajevo." And here we can see signatures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce page number 3 in e-court. Now you can see two versions of the same document. In the English it says: "80, 17." There is a date and a signature. And here it says four pages and before we saw seven pages. Where are the missing pages? It says 17 -- and can the lower bottom corner be zoomed in, please. In the English translation -- or, rather, the original which contains the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it is unclear for the Court Usher, but also for me, to which part of this it document you're referring. Could you repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the lower right corner of the English original be zoomed in. There is signature, and it also says "P-a-g-e 17," which stands for page 17. And now we can see that part is blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness please explain how come that we are looking at page 17 with the signature of one of the participants, whereas only four pages of the document have been disclosed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is not a document that I have been involved in at all. So we can maybe try to find the original document and try to find the translation and see what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a copy of the original, and you told us last time that you had seen this document when we discussed the signature in the left-hand side corner and when I asked you whose signature that was. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen the document. It was in reference to a tape that matched with a tape that we had picked up -- been given in April of 1998. This is a document that was produced by another team that searched -- consensually searched the barracks in Sarajevo in October of 2000. I left the Tribunal in July of 2000, but I have seen this document, but I cannot account for the discrepancy in the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see 17 pages, or did you see only four as it says in here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember for certain. It's possible that I only saw four. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that some of the tapes on the list on page 1 of the four containing a total of 20 items, is it possible that the pages from 4 through 17 have not been disclosed to the Defence and that they have therefore not been used at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think there's no issue with respect to this particular document. The ERN range indicates five pages. If you look at the very first page of the document, it indicates that there is an attached four page -- four-page inventory, which is exactly what we see before us. While I cannot offer you at the moment an explanation for why it indicates pages 7 -- 16 through 19 on the attached inventory, I think from the ERN range and from the face of the document itself, it is quite clear that it is a four-page document. It's a four-page instrument, and that's both reflected in the B/C/S and the English translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, we saw the English and the B/C/S version of this document. It was not marked for identification pending translation, but it was received as an exhibit, just for the record. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the record, I'm asking whether the ERN number is the Prosecutor's name, the court's -- the Prosecutor's number, the court's number, or is it the number that was used by the BiH Army when it handed over the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Maybe you can answer this question, because as you've just told us, you saw this document.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: ERN numbers are placed on documents by the Tribunal. And more specifically, by the Evidence Section of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that section part of the Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor, the Registry? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it falls under the Registry, but I'm not absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, on page 3 of this document that we see before us, the first item in the first column reads: "Document number: 100124. Number of pages: 1. Date: 16 October. Description: A box 100 centimetres X 75 centimetres X 50 centimetres containing numerous audiotapes and a number of audio magnetic reels." I'm interested in the last part which refers to numerous audiotapes and a number of audio magnetic reels. The words that I quoted I quoted to provide you with complete information as to where that can be found. My question is this: What is the difference between audiotapes and audio magnetic reels, and do both items refer to intercepted conversations? So what is the difference between audio tapes and audio magnetic reels? I repeat that part of -- of my question. And I repeat once again, whether all of the two types of media have to do with intercepted conversations.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to speculate here because I was not present when these were taken into custody, and I have not looked at all of them, and I have not listened to all of them. Maybe on the left-hand side if in the B/C/S version of the document I could just look at the first sentence of that entry on the 16th of October. But I believe that the magnetic reels would refer to the reel-to-reel tapes like the UHER reel-to-reel tapes. I'm sorry, the first page of the B/C/S document, on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see it in the English version. It's the first passage on the right. Could you please tell me what contents were found on those magnetic reels. Did you inspect all of them, and would you be able to tell us? Would you be able to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe I just mentioned that I wasn't present at the Tribunal when these were seized and that I have not looked at all of them and have not listened to all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain, do you know what UHER uses, whether it uses cassettes or tapes and so on and so forth, or some other kinds of tapes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UHER uses round magnetic tapes. I guess magnetic. I don't know. Round tracks; right? "Trake."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you testified in the Krstic and Popovic cases, did you have an opportunity to listen to those tapes again and to see them again, or was it somebody else who was involved in the analysis of the material after having listened to it again?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did listen to the material and testified about it in the Popovic case, but not in the Krstic, to my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we're talking about numerous tapes, reels and cassettes. Could you please explain, would all those fall under UHER and whether any other types of equipment were used to record intercepted conversations? If those existed, were they available to you, and where can they be found? Where were they recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce page 3 in the English translation for the benefit of the witness, so that the witness could see that there is a reference to all the different types of media cassettes, tapes, and reels, and we would like the witness to tell us whether she had all those made available to her, whether she was able to use all that. Could you please blow-up, for the benefit of the witness, the first paragraph under 1 in the English language. I would like the witness to be able to see that part better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please look at line 1 and you will see that everything that I have mentioned in my question is referred to in here.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was not present when these tapes -- is the recording working? My microphones don't sound like they're working, or headphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can't hear you through the headphones as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hello? Are things working? That sounds better. So I have not had an opportunity to look at all of the items that you mention. As I've said, I left the Tribunal in July of 2000 and was not present when these were seized. I listened to tape 49 in this set, which was a reel-to-reel tape. I have not examined all of the other recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, when you answered the Prosecutor's questions during the examination-in-chief, could you please confirm for us that tapes from 1 to 49 MBs are -- and I am quoting what you said on page 4993: "I did not inspect all the cassettes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the -- could Mr. Tolimir please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Why you did not control the contents of all the tapes to see whether they correspond to the typed transcripts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just with respect to your quotation of my statement that, "I did not inspect all the cassettes, "I'm not sure that I said I did not inspect all of the cassettes. I may have said the reel-to-reels or the audio recordings or something to that effect. I did not inspect all of them simply as a matter of a lack of time, and also, they did not -- my understanding is that this material does not all relate to the events of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to clarify one thing, and that was with respect to the witnesses direct testimony. What she was referring to in this particular document is actually on the following page and it's under item 100132, and that relates to 98 audio magnetic reels as opposed to cassettes, as you can see is indicated under this item, 100124, although they came from the same box, and those are referenced also under item 100132, which specifically references cassette materials that were contained under item 100124 and items contained under 100135. So just so that we're specific as to what the reference was in direct concerning this witness's interaction with this material or the materials that she actually did review and listen to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you follow this recommendation of Mr. Vanderpuye to make a distinction between the two portions of documents received and as stated in the document, then it would be appreciated, and continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since the transcript has not properly recorded my question, I would like to repeat the question, and maybe it will become clearer. Everything will become clearer. Please, for the benefit of the witness, could the court please produce page 4993, line 5 of the transcript, and she will see that I quoted her words. And that is the transcript page dated 7 September. And now I'm going to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When it comes to the diskettes that you received from the BiH Army, to the Prosecutor's questions -- question whether you can confirm that those diskettes from -- of 1.94 MBs, and that has been erroneously translated, referred to the intercepted communications from January through December 1995. And you said on page 4993, line 5 of the transcript: "I did not inspect every single diskette." My question was this: Could you please tell us why you did not inspect the contents of every of the diskettes? Did I properly quote your words back to you? Since you asked for it, now you can look at the transcript line yourself. We see line number 5, page 4993, that's where I was quoting from. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't look at every diskette and every entry in every diskette, again because of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. On page 6371, line 20, in the Popovic case you are recorded as saying that, firstly, you couldn't open the diskette. My question is this: Did you manage to get hold of the contents of those diskettes subsequently, or in other words, were you able to open the files contained on those diskettes, and if you did, how did you manage to do that subsequently?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we received two diskettes which we were unable to open internally, and then we later, after I left, received additional diskettes which the Office of the Prosecutor or the technical people were able to open and to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the diskettes were not damaged but that they were encrypted? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They may have been encrypted, but certainly we couldn't open them. That was, for me, the main point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And later on, did you learn what programmes were used when the diskettes were uploaded and what programmes did the BH Army use? Were you able to establish what computer programmes were used on those diskettes, and if you did, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not learn what programmes were used by the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you every learn whose encryption, or whose code was used on those diskettes? Did you ever investigate that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We received the diskettes after I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are the diskettes still here at the Tribunal, and were they opened by using the encryption code that the BiH Army used, or are these diskettes still unavailable for use? Are they still unaccessible?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they're here within the OTP and that they are accessible. And available for use. I don't know how they were opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I said that the BiH Army used Lelic's [Realtime transcript read in error "Lilic's"] code, Professor Lelic's encryption code. That was not recorded previously. That's why I'm repeating it. But it doesn't really matter, because you will no longer be involved in that ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to correct the record. On page 56, line 3, it says "Lilic" instead of "Lelic." It is Lelic's encryption code rather than Lilic's encryption code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is now recorded properly. Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Mr. Tolimir, I think it is the right time for our second break, and after the break we will continue. We adjourn and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to advise the Court that translations have been uploaded for P838, P826B, and P826A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think they will be now exhibits. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you personally visit any of the facilities which intercepted the communications of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I visited both sites; one on the 21st of April, 1998, and the second on the 22nd of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time in 1998, did you see how radio communications are intercepted, how that is done?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you able to see the equipment that was used by the intercepting team of the BH Army, and if you did see it, could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some of the UHER machines. I saw some of the -- whether they were receivers or transmitters I couldn't tell you, and some of the antennas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have seen some of the antennae and some witnesses here said they had made improvised antennas using sticks and rope and wash basins, were you able to see if they were factory-produced antennae or makeshift ones?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am no expert on antennas. Some of them looked like they were store-bought antennas. Some of them looked like they were made out of stop signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that's how they looked, some store bought, others made of stop signs, was it possible with equipment of that sort to monitor radio communications at the time of Srebrenica and Zepa events with any success?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not an expert in this field. That's why Jack Hunter was asked to come and make the analysis. In talking with the radio operators, they explained not only that they made antennas but that they were able to make other pieces of equipment in order to make it all work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, do you have any report made by Mr. Jack Hunter, whom we referred to several times today about radio communication systems, audio recordings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are really running out of time now, so I won't be showing P287. I'll just tell you what it is. It's an aerial photograph of the playing field in Kasaba. You said it was a play field, not a football stadium. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it was a playground or a football field, a soccer field, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were explaining that on page 5027, lines 6 through 13, you said, and I'll quote to remind you: "We used photographs, aerial photographs, that correspond to events that were discussed in intercepted communications." And you were later shown one photograph, and when you saw it you said: "Q. Did you consider in thinking about reliability and authenticity these two photographs? In other words, when determining reliability and authenticity, did you consider these two photographs?" You said: "Yes." "Q. Did you consider this particular aerial photograph in relation to these two intercepts?" And you answered: "The date and the time and the fact that the analyst provided information about this picture indicate that the triangle or rectangle on this photograph represents people." Did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Close enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You can look up the transcript later. I did not add anything. Could you answer this question: The photograph such as the one showing the playground, which is an aerial satellite image, can it be a factor in deciding about the authenticity of an intercept, and can it be used as a basis in determining that an intercept made by the BH Army or the US Army or any other agency was made by that particular agency?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We used aerial imagery in order to authenticate some of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber how it is that one can establish who made an intercept based on -- on such a photograph?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not possible to determine who made the intercept based on the photograph. It's simply possible to compare the substance of the intercept with the aerial image. After "determine" there should be the word "who."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why would photographs be used to do this when it was general knowledge and there were witnesses, participants of these events who were able to provide testimony?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to use information that would be considered independent and that did not come from Bosnian witnesses so that there wouldn't be a question about, well, you're using a Bosnian witness to corroborate a Bosnian intercept. Therefore, we tried to use and we did use information that was independent and outside of the purview of the Bosnian authorities. Therefore, we used VRS documents, VRS -- or telephone books from Republika Srpska, aerial imagery from the United States, and other sorts of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at the time of the events in Srebrenica that you investigated there were drones up in the air and they do electronic surveillance and monitor radio and other communications? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it at the time, but in the intercepted communication it seemed that the VRS was aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that analysts and experts knew that, and were they able to direct you to the reports made by these drones that are more reliable than any photograph could possibly be, and did you use such reports?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by reports from drones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me read to you and let's show on the screen P128, a document tendered by the Prosecution. It's probably a document you read before, because you testified about similar documents. It says in paragraph 1: "There is a drone in the airspace conducting observation and jamming of radio communications. It has been here since 0500 hours and has probably recorded certain features and movements. The following measures therefore need to be taken," et cetera, et cetera. This is just the first paragraph of a document that I wrote on the 14th of July, 1995, and I signed it as Assistant Commander for Intelligence, Major-General Zdravko Tolimir. Now, looking at this and since you've spoken about the contents of similar documents in your evidence-in-chief, can you tell us whether you are familiar with this particular document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. It's the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at item 3, please, item 3 of this warning I issued to units. It says: "In addition to wire communications, establish also all radio communications." Do you see that the document says that wire communications should be used because there was an unmanned aircraft in the air? Were you or experts like Mr. Hunter aware that unmanned aircraft were recording the communications between various participants?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your evidence you mentioned an analyst who provided the necessary information about this photograph. Can you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P214, please. And it should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that this document is not confidential, so that we don't see the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In that case I will read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a letter sent by the US embassy to Mr. McCloskey, the Senior Trial Attorney. Paragraph 3 on page 1 in English, and it's page 2 in Serbian. We will see page 2 in Serbian in a few moments but you can start reading already. Look at the second page -- second sentence here. It says: "The United States made clear, however, that the OTP was not authorised to discuss in courtroom proceedings any information relating to the technical or analytical sources, methods, or capabilities of the systems, organisations or personnel used to collect, analyse, or produce these imagery-derived products." So this is evidence that falls under Rule 70. Were you aware of these restrictions when you were -- restrictions on the use of material such as aerial photographs and other material provided by the US government?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that there were sensitivities around information that was provided by the US government. However, I would not have used the aerial imagery in the authentication material had it not been approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted from the document, and now I'm asking you this: Were you forbidden as a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor to share information about the authenticity or reliability of, for example, the photo that you saw, which I didn't show, and the information that it contains anywhere outside of this courtroom or the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wondered if Mr. Tolimir could be a little bit more specific as to the time-frame that he's talking about, because obviously if the restrictions were in place, then they applied as opposed to other periods of time. So if he can be more specific, I think we can get a more informative answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is it possible to be a little bit more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can be more specific, Your Honour. In the previous question, I said, "While you were an employee of the Tribunal." You can check the record if you wish. But let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this observed by you while you were an employee of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the restriction observed by me while I was an employee of the Tribunal? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The question was whether you were forbidden as a representative of the office of the Tribunal to share information about the material that you obtained from the government of the United States of America in the spirit of the material that I have just quoted from.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only time that I recall sharing, to use your word, information of this nature was in the Krstic trial, and I had authorisation from the Office of the Prosecutor to use, I think, one or two images. My -- my further memory is that Jean-Rene Ruez had authorisation to use aerial imagery in his testimony in that trial and in subsequent trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Since you used the images in the Krstic case, as you have just told us, did anybody explain to you the electronic dots and black shadows on the electronic imagery? Did anybody explain to you as to how to decipher the photos, how to -- how to read them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was explained to Jean-Rene Ruez, who then explained it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us now, when it comes to the checking of reliability and authenticity of intercepts, what would be more reliable and relevant, an aerial image or a satellite image of the same area?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always told to refer to these as aerial images. I don't know the difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you forbidden to say in court, in keeping with the information of the government of the USA that I read from, to use the electronic imagery of a pilotless aircraft or not? Maybe you can't answer in open session. We can move into private session if you want to answer my question in private session.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer, so it doesn't -- we can stay in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In view of your answer, I'm going to have a different question for you now. How did you select from the material in -- for authentication? Was that a random sample or did you consider some of the intercepts particularly significant, which is why you tried to check and control those particular ones by contrasting them with other materials, and did you ever cross-check any of the intercepts with the imagery obtained from a pilotless aircraft?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the last part of your question because I don't know the answer. With respect to how intercepts were selected for independent authentication, I can explain a little bit the process. After having gone through the material for quite some time and being familiar with different information from the investigation, like notes from UN officials or aerial imagery or captured VRS documents, when I or members of the team would see something that corroborated an intercept we would simply file it, not knowing, not having a real plan for what we would eventually do with it but as a matter of interest and importance for us to gain confidence in the authenticity and the reliability of that body of work. So it was a selection that was ultimately made, and what I aimed to do was to get as broad a selection as possible using a variety of independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5028, lines from 4 to -- through 6, you said: "It would be impossible to carry out an independent authentication of every intercepted conversation." My question is this: Why is it not possible to test the authenticity of each of the intercepts that are of some significance for this trial in view of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't. It's possible to corroborate, I think, many of them at this point given the number of captured documents that we have, the number of notes from UN officials, the aerial imagery, and if we wanted to include witness statements, also witness statements. I think we -- we could corroborate a lot of them, but -- yeah. I mean, I -- I can look at one here that -- that says, you know, a Russian from Crimea came here. He has men who would come here in order to gain combat experience. To my knowledge, right now we don't have anything that corroborates that particular intercept. If we had additional documentation from the VRS, it's quite possible that we could corroborate the same way that we were able to corroborate the conversation from the 20th of April, 1995, about the two Polish volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we have mentioned the issue of volunteers, the document that was sent to Popovic and Nikolic, as you said, was it actually sent to the personnel officials who were in charge of the replenishment of the units?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Jovicic was the personnel person in the Zvornik Brigade and then that he was dispatching Polish volunteers further to Zvornik Brigade, to the security branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just spontaneously told us the name of the person, and my next question is this: The intercepts, all of them, or at least some of them were first made public in the press and the media and only then were they handed over to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- do you know that some of the intercepted conversations were first published in the media, in the press, and only then handed over to the Tribunal? You can see and you can tell that looking at the dates showing when they were handed over to you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we would have -- I would have to see the articles that you're referring to. It is true that there were intercepts that were published in the media, but I don't recall that they were published before we had access to them. I could be wrong, but we'd have to take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It would take us too far, and I don't have that much time left. I have only a couple of questions for you. Bearing in mind what you've just told us, my next question is this, and especially in view of the fact that you said the intercepted communications were intercepted in realtime, if that indeed had been the case, if they had been intercepted in realtime, wouldn't it have been logical and obvious to disclose their contents to -- contents to the Security Council, international monitors, and the Tribunal and not to hide them for three or four years perhaps before you got hold of them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Bosnian authorities would probably be better placed to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But what about you? What about your opinion? Wouldn't it have been better that even before the Dayton Accords or any other resolutions on Bosnia that was passed after the war that this information had been publicly disclosed and that the internationally -- international community and local community had been aware of that information? What do you think? What's your opinion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've given my view before, which is that the war was going on at the time, and it made sense for them not to disclose the information to us. I -- I remember one intercept operator saying that at some point during the war they had disclosed a particular intercept, and after that -- and it was one that he had intercepted, and after that he remembers feeling somewhat regretful over the fact that the intercept was made public, because then it let the VRS know that they had the capabilities to intercept the conversations. As for disclosing this kind of information to international organisations, to the UN and others, I don't know. I mean, you know better than I do, I think, that there were drones, I've learned today, and other means and methods that governments had to know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber will be the judge of who suffers more, an individual or a state. I have two more questions for you. You have spoken about notebooks, and my question is this: Did you ever have those notebooks in your hands? Did you help BiH Army members to get ahold of those notebooks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was not present during the mission when members of the Office of the Prosecutor were with members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and when the notebooks were found. And I've always only had professional contacts with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and with the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about the first part of the question: "Did you ever have those notebooks in your hands"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I worked with the notebooks very much once they came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, but I was also always very protective of those notebooks. We photocopied them, we worked off of photocopies of them, and treated those notebooks like precious objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were employed by the Tribunal did you ever enroll in master's studies in Italy, and while you were in Italy, did you ever send any notebooks to Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never enrolled in master's studies in Italy, and I did not send any notebooks from Italy to Bosnia. I don't know whether you're confusing a trip that some investigators and I took to Italy to have ligatures examined by the police in Rome, but to my memory, it had nothing to do with notebooks. I do, however, speak Italian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't say "master's studies," but "master's studies" [as interpreted]. Maybe this has been misinterpreted or mis-recorded. However, you answered my question. We had witnesses here who were intercept operators, and they told us that they handed over handwritten notes to the representatives of the Tribunal. Do you know if anybody carried out an expert analysis of those handwritten notes? Was it ever done? Who did it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which handwritten notes you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The operators who recorded conversations in the notebooks, did any graphologists analyse their handwriting? Are you privy to the results of such a graphologic analysis if any was done?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the question now. I believe it was sometime in the spring of 1999 when we were getting ready to begin interviews with the intercept operators that we developed just small one-page forms that would allow the -- allow us to take writing samples from the various intercept operators. And that was done so that we could easily, more easily, identify the operators who had written the conversations that we considered at the time to be most important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the graphology testing of the handwritten notes that were handed over to you by the operators? Was it ever done?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was ever done by the Office of the Prosecutor, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 70 of the transcript of 10 September this year in this case, that is lines 8 through 9, you said: "When I first started working with the material --"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "When I first started working with the material, I had a lot of concern with regard to the reliability and authenticity of the material." My question: Based on what you stated, did you speak about the way you analysed the material, and can you please share your concerns with us with regard to the authenticity of the material and also the concerns you had with regard to the material's reliability? So what were your concerns with regard to the authenticity, on the one hand, and the reliability of the material on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think my concerns and the concerns of the team are the same concerns that you have, that the Judges have, and that anybody else would have that was working with material that was purported to be radio intercepts captured at the time of significant events. Within the team, sometimes we would say - and I'm being perfectly candid - what if this is all made up? What if people were sitting in a basement writing this stuff out? We took this very seriously. We dug very deeply into it. We left, in my view, absolutely no stone unturned in validating the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: With regard to the concerns that you've just mentioned, do you have a list of some other concerns you had with regard to the authenticity and reliability? And thank you for your answers. Thank you for your fair testimony. I wish you a pleasant stay, and this brings my examination to an end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There was one last question, and for fairness reasons you should answer this question. Do you have a list of some other concerns you had with regard to the authenticity and reliability?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye, we are running out of time, but you must have the chance for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I don't think -- I do have a brief re-examination in mind, and I don't think I can complete it in the time that we have and I see that we're over. I also wanted to mention this just in case Mr. Tolimir hasn't completed his cross-examination, which I see that he has, but if he hasn't, I would ask to be allowed to re-examine tomorrow. It shouldn't take more than 10 or 15 minutes, but I think it's more time than we can spare now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is the best way. We are running out of time. The courtroom will be used by another Chamber, so that we have to adjourn now and sorry for that.
